procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 12.01.2017 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Bail Application No. 2160 of 2016, directing the release of the accused on bail.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused applied for bail before the Bombay High Court after the Sessions Court, Pune rejected their bail applications. The High Court granted bail, noting that the deceased's 'fault' was only that he belonged to another religion and that the accused had no personal animus against the deceased and seemed to be provoked in the name of religion.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the High Court's reasoning for granting bail appeared to be biased. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, restored the bail applications to the file of the High Court, directed the High Court to hear the matters afresh, and ordered that two of the accused be taken into custody if they did not surrender within one week. The parties were directed to appear before the High Court on 16.02.2018, and the High Court was directed to decide the bail applications at the earliest, but no later than 6 weeks from the parties' appearance.

directions: The impugned order(s) are set aside.
The bail applications are restored to the file of the High Court to hear the matters afresh.
The parties are directed to appear before the High Court on 16.02.2018.
The bail applications may be decided at the earliest, in any case, not later than 6 weeks from the date the parties appear before the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether bail can be granted to an accused in a murder case on the grounds that they had no personal animus against the deceased and were provoked in the name of religion, with the victim's religion being considered a factor in favour of the accused.

facts: The accused were part of a group that allegedly targeted and assaulted the victim, Shaikh Mohsin, with bats and sticks, resulting in his death.
The prosecution's case was that the victim was targeted solely because he belonged to a particular religious community.
The Trial Court had rejected the accused's bail applications, finding prima facie evidence of a conspiracy to kill members of a certain community.
The High Court overturned this and granted bail, reasoning that the accused had no personal animus against the deceased and were provoked in the name of religion.
Crucially, the High Court stated, "The fault of the deceased was only that he belonged to another religion. I consider this factor in favour of the applicants/accused."
law: The fact that a victim belongs to a certain community cannot be considered a mitigating circumstance or a justification for any assault, much less a murder.
Courts, being conscious of the country's pluralistic composition, cannot make observations that may appear to be coloured with a bias for or against any community.
A decision to grant bail in a murder case must be based on a proper discussion of all relevant factors, not on a single, flawed reason.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning for granting bail to be legally unsustainable and deeply problematic.
It held that the High Court's observation—that the victim's only "fault" was his religion and that this was a factor "in favour" of the accused—was an unacceptable justification for the crime.
The Supreme Court stated that such remarks appear "coloured with a bias" and, regardless of the judge's intent, are vulnerable to criticism and cannot be sustained.

The Court also noted that the High Court's order failed to properly discuss other relevant factors for granting or withholding bail in a murder case, focusing almost exclusively on this flawed reasoning.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's grounds for granting bail. It concluded that using the victim's religion as a mitigating factor in favour of the accused was a biased and legally impermissible justification for murder. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and sent the bail applications back to the High Court for a fresh hearing on the merits.

arguments.issue_text: Whether bail can be granted to an accused in a murder case on the grounds that they had no personal animus against the deceased and were provoked in the name of religion, with the victim's religion being considered a factor in favour of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's reasoning for granting bail is flawed and amounts to a justification for murder.
The fact that the deceased belonged to a certain community cannot be considered a mitigating circumstance or a factor in favour of the accused.
The High Court's observation that 'the fault of the deceased was only that he belonged to another religion' is improper and appears to be coloured with a bias.
The prosecution's case is that the accused were part of a conspiracy to kill members of a certain community and targeted the victim for this reason, which is a serious offense.
respondent_arguments: Bail should be granted because the accused had no personal animus against the deceased.
The accused were provoked in the name of religion, which should be considered a mitigating factor.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The fact that a victim of a crime belongs to a particular religious community cannot be considered a mitigating circumstance or a justification for the offense when deciding on a bail application. A judicial order that relies on such reasoning is unsustainable as it may appear to be colored with bias.
obiter: Our observations shall not be construed as comments on the merits of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's primary reason for granting bail—that the accused had no personal animus and were provoked by religion, with the victim's religion being considered a mitigating factor—is an unacceptable justification for murder. The fact that a deceased person belonged to a certain community can never be a justification for any assault, much less a murder. Such reasoning is unsustainable, especially when the High Court stated that the "fault of the deceased was only that he belonged to another religion" and considered this a factor in favor of the accused.
legal_tests_applied: While not a formal test, the court applied a standard of judicial propriety, holding that bail decisions cannot be based on reasoning that appears biased or justifies a crime based on the victim's community identity.

The court noted the High Court's failure to apply the standard analysis for bail in a murder case, observing that "there is little discussion on the other relevant factors relating to granting or withholding bail in a murder case."
policy_considerations: A court, being fully conscious of the pluralistic composition of the country, cannot make observations that may appear to be colored with a bias for or against any community when dealing with the rights of various communities.

Judicial reasoning, even if not intended to be biased, is unacceptable if its words are "clearly vulnerable to such criticism" as they can be misunderstood as a justification for a communally motivated murder.
